name: Decisions That Stay With People
title: Decisions That Stay With People
answer: Decisions that stay with people means AI may inform a decision about a child or an employee, but a named person makes the call and can explain it. This matters because tools that produce scores and flags can look official and quietly take over judgment, and because the order of the work shapes whether unfair calls get corrected. Schools need people to decide first and use AI as a check, with a clear route to human review.

crumbs.name: What AI Can and Cannot Do

sections.body: The idea is a simple rule that runs through this Volume: AI can inform a decision about a child or an employee, but a named person makes it and can explain it. The rule sounds obvious, yet it is easy to lose once a tool starts producing scores and flags that look official. The problem it solves is the drift of real judgment into software that appears authoritative. Figure 1.6 applies the rule to seven decisions every school makes. The order of the work matters too, because people rarely fix unfair decisions when the machine calls first and they are only supposed to correct it.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, people form their own judgment first and then use AI to check it, rather than letting the machine make the first call. The Texas scoring program shows what shared work can look like: the automated engine scores written answers first, people rescore about a quarter of them, and answers the engine is unsure about, or that are unusual, go straight to human scorers. When AI touches a decision that matters, people need a clear way to ask for a human review. Buying a tool is also a decision about people, as the Los Angeles Unified story shows. The text does not give grade band examples for this idea.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book reports three online experiments with adults in which a machine made the first call and a person was supposed to correct it. In those experiments, people rarely fixed unfair decisions and often went along with them, while the problem went away when the person decided first and the machine served as the check (Krugel et al., 2023). The study did not involve schools, but the lesson travels. The Texas scoring program is described from the Texas Tribune (2024), and the Los Angeles Unified chatbot story from EdSurge (2024), where a contract worth about $6 million was launched in 2024, about $3 million was paid, and the tool was shut down within months when the vendor collapsed.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits and risks are set out plainly. Even with shared work, some educators still questioned the Texas results, which is part of the lesson that people need a clear way to ask for a human review when AI touches a decision that matters. The Los Angeles Unified case shows the risk of depending on a vendor, since families were left asking where student data had gone after the shutdown. The decisions that stay with a person are the calls about a child or an employee, which a named person makes and can explain. The text does not set out further rules, so the guardrail is the rule itself and the review path it requires.
